questions.q: Why is the region formed by India and its six neighbours called a 'subcontinent'?
questions.a: The chapter says it is a subcontinent since it is part of the continent of Asia. The other options invent a separate continent or confuse it with a direction or a single feature.
o: Because it is a part of the continent of Asia
Because it is a separate, smaller continent of its own
Because it lies to the south of the Himalayan range
Because it is the region around the Thar Desert

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT named in the chapter as one of the neighbours that, with India, form the Indian Subcontinent?
questions.a: The chapter lists Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar. Afghanistan appears only as a Himalayan country, so it is the odd one out.
o: Afghanistan
Bangladesh
Sri Lanka
Myanmar

questions.q: In size, the chapter says India is the
questions.a: The chapter states that India is the seventh-largest country in the world and a part of Asia.
o: seventh-largest country in the world
second-largest country in the world
sixth-largest country in the world
eighth-largest country in the world

questions.q:
Match each feature in Column A with the side of India it bounds in Column B.
Column A: 1. Himalayan Mountain range  2. Thar Desert and Arabian Sea  3. Indian Ocean  4. Bay of Bengal
Column B: a. southern boundary  b. eastern boundary  c. northern barrier  d. western limits
questions.a: Himalayas - north; Thar and Arabian Sea - west; Indian Ocean - south; Bay of Bengal - east. The distractors swap south with east or north with west.

questions.q: Kabir's cousin in Colombo says, 'We also belong to the Indian Subcontinent.' Which reason from the chapter supports her claim?
questions.a: Sri Lanka is named with Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan and Myanmar as part of the subcontinent. It is not one of India's own island groups, nor in the Himalayan zone.
o: It is one of six neighbours that form the subcontinent with India
It is part of the island region within India's own territory
It lies at the foot of the Himalayan mountain zone, as India does
It lies on the Bay of Bengal coast of India itself, in the east

questions.q: Ananya labels a blank outline map and puts 'Lakshadweep' and 'Andaman and Nicobar' in one box. Under which of the five regions in the chapter does the box belong?
questions.a: Both groups are islands, the fifth region in the chapter's list. Putting them with the southern peninsula is a common slip because they lie near its coasts.
o: The islands
The southern peninsula
The great mountain zone
The desert region

questions.q:
Read the statements about India's location.
1. India is the seventh-largest country in the world and is a part of Asia.
2. The Indian Subcontinent consists only of India and the countries that touch the Himalayas.
3. The Himalayan Mountain range stands as a natural barrier in the north of India.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are from the chapter. 2 is false: Sri Lanka and Myanmar are in the subcontinent, and the group is not defined by touching the Himalayas.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India is the seventh-largest country in the world.
Reason (R): The Himalayan Mountain range stands as a natural barrier in the north of India.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the Himalayas being a barrier says nothing about the country's size, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Name the natural features that bound India on the west, south and east. (b) The chapter says these features 'create a separation'. Separation from what, and which three aspects of India did this help to shape?
questions.a: (a) Thar Desert and Arabian Sea (west), Indian Ocean (south), Bay of Bengal (east). (b) Separation from the rest of the continent; it shaped India's climate, culture and history.
s: Part (a): Thar and Arabian Sea in the west, Indian Ocean in the south, Bay of Bengal in the east
Part (b): separation from the rest of the continent, shaping climate, culture and history

questions.q: What is the Indian Subcontinent? Name any four countries, other than India, that are part of it.
questions.a: The region formed by India and its neighbours, a part of the continent of Asia. Any four of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, Myanmar.
s: Defines it as India with its neighbours, forming part of Asia
Names four correct neighbours

questions.q: (a) What do the different colours on the physical map at the end of the book stand for? (b) Why must a reader look at the legend before deciding that a coloured patch is a mountain and not a plain?
questions.a: (a) Different altitudes (heights of the land). (b) The same map shows mountains, plains and plateaus only through the colours, so the legend tells which colour means which height.
s: Part (a): colours show altitudes (heights)
Part (b): the legend is the key that links a colour to a height, so landforms cannot be read without it

questions.q: (a) Who was the first Indian astronaut to go into space, and what did he reply when asked how India looks from space? (b) What does the line he quoted say about how Indians see their land?
questions.a: (a) Rakesh Sharma replied 'Sare jahan se achchha'. (b) It means 'better than the whole world', an expression of pride in India and its geography.
s: Part (a): Rakesh Sharma and the line 'Sare jahan se achchha'
Part (b): meaning 'better than the whole world', pride in the land

questions.q: (a) What did Sri Aurobindo say India's geography gives it? (b) Which feature, mentioned in the chapter, separates India from the rest of the continent in the north?
questions.a: (a) It makes India appear quite distinct from other countries and gives it a certain national character. (b) The Himalayan Mountain range, a natural barrier.
s: Part (a): distinct from other countries, a certain national character
Part (b): the Himalayan range as the northern barrier

questions.q: Leela says, 'India and the Indian Subcontinent mean the same thing, because the subcontinent is named after India.' Is she right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Only partly. India does give its name to the subcontinent, but the subcontinent is a bigger region: India together with Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar, a part of Asia. India is one country in it.
s: Accepts the naming fact and gives a verdict of not the same
Subcontinent includes six neighbours as well as India
Subcontinent is a part of Asia while India is one country

questions.q: A student lists the five regions of India as: the great mountain zone, the plains of the Ganga and the Indus, the desert region, the Deccan Plateau and the coasts. Find the two entries that do not match the chapter's list, correct them and say which three are right.
questions.a: Wrong: 'the Deccan Plateau' should be 'the southern peninsula'; 'the coasts' should be 'the islands'. Right: the great mountain zone, the plains of the Ganga and the Indus, the desert region.
s: Corrects the Deccan Plateau entry to the southern peninsula
Corrects the coasts entry to the islands
Names the three correct entries

questions.q: India has been called a 'mini-continent'. Using the chapter's five regions, give three reasons why this name fits.
questions.a: Within one country it holds a great mountain zone, the Ganga-Indus plains, a desert region, a southern peninsula and islands; they differ in climate, soil, plants, animals and ways of living, as in different parts of a continent. The chapter says the diverse features created a variety of conditions.
s: Names at least three different regions inside India
Notes the variety in conditions such as soil, flora, fauna or life
Links the variety to the size and diversity of the country, as a continent has

questions.q: 'Nature has drawn India's boundary on every side.' Justify this statement, naming the feature on each side and what the boundaries have done for India.
questions.a: North: the Himalayan range like a wall; west: Thar Desert and Arabian Sea; south: Indian Ocean; east: Bay of Bengal. Together they separate India from the rest of the continent and have played a crucial role in shaping its climate, culture and history.
s: North and west features correctly named
South and east features correctly named
Explains the separation from the rest of the continent
Links the boundaries to climate, culture and history

questions.q: Compare 'India', 'the Indian Subcontinent' and 'Asia' and analyse why the chapter uses the word 'sub' in the second term.
questions.a: India is a country, the seventh-largest in the world. The Indian Subcontinent is the region formed by India with Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar. Asia is the continent that holds all of these. It is called a subcontinent since it is part of the continent of Asia.
s: India described as a country, seventh-largest in the world
Subcontinent described with the six neighbours
Asia described as the continent containing both
Explains 'sub' as being part of Asia

questions.q:
A geography club in a Nagpur school has Rs 3,000 for wall panels titled 'Why India stands apart in Asia'. Panel prices: natural boundaries Rs 1,800; five regions Rs 1,500; neighbours of India Rs 900. The neighbours panel will list every country that forms the subcontinent with India.
(a) How many countries will the neighbours panel list, and why does the chapter call this group a 'sub'continent?
(b) What must the boundaries panel show to explain why India appears 'quite distinct' from the rest of the continent?
(c) Which pairs of panels fit within the budget, and what does each pair cost?
(d) Which affordable pair best suits the title, and why?
questions.a: (a) Six (Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, Myanmar); it is a part of the continent of Asia. (b) The Himalayas (north), Thar Desert and Arabian Sea (west), Indian Ocean (south) and Bay of Bengal (east), which separate India from the rest of the continent. (c) Boundaries + neighbours = 1800 + 900 = Rs 2,700; regions + neighbours = 1500 + 900 = Rs 2,400; boundaries + regions = Rs 3,300, over budget. (d) Boundaries + neighbours: the title is about standing apart, and the boundaries are what separate India and shaped its climate, culture and history, while regions show variety inside India.
s: Part (a): six countries, part of Asia
Part (b): natural boundary features and the separation they create
Part (c): boundaries+neighbours Rs 2,700 and regions+neighbours Rs 2,400 fit; boundaries+regions Rs 3,300 does not
Part (d): boundaries with neighbours, justified by separation shaping climate, culture, history

questions.q:
In a school quiz the question was: 'Name the countries that, with India, form the Indian Subcontinent.' Team Kaveri wrote Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar. Team Narmada wrote those six and also Afghanistan and China. The quiz master gives 1 mark for each correct name and takes away 1 mark for each wrong name. Team Narmada appeals, saying the Himalayas also run through Afghanistan and China.
(a) What marks does each team get?
(b) Which two names did Team Narmada add wrongly, according to the chapter's list?
(c) Is the appeal's fact correct, and does it make those two countries part of the subcontinent?
(d) Should the quiz master accept the appeal? Give your decision with reasons.
questions.a: (a) Kaveri: 6 correct = 6 marks. Narmada: 6 correct - 2 wrong = 4 marks. (b) Afghanistan and China. (c) The fact is correct: the range stretches across six countries including China and Afghanistan. But the subcontinent is the group of India and the six neighbours the chapter names, not every country the range touches. (d) Reject: the question asked for the subcontinent, whose members the chapter lists, and the Himalayan fact answers a different question. The master may offer a fresh question on the Himalayan countries.
s: Part (a): Kaveri 6, Narmada 6 - 2 = 4
Part (b): Afghanistan and China
Part (c): Himalayas do stretch across six countries, but the subcontinent list is separate
Part (d): rejects the appeal, with reasoning

questions.q: The word 'Himalaya' comes from two Sanskrit words. What does it mean?
questions.a: Hima means snow and alaya means abode, so 'abode of snow'. 'Cow's mouth' is Gaumukh, 'Water Tower' is a nickname and 'wall' is a comparison in the text.
o: Abode of snow
Cow's mouth
Water tower
Wall of the north

questions.q: Which range is the outermost and lowest of the three Himalayan ranges?
questions.a: The Shivalik Hills (Outer Himalayas) are the lowest. Himadri is the highest, Himachal lies between, and the Sahyadri Hills are the northern Western Ghats, not Himalayan.
o: Shivalik Hills
Himachal
Himadri
Sahyadri Hills

questions.q: About how many years ago did the Indian landmass collide with Eurasia to start building the Himalayas?
questions.a: The chapter says about 50 million years ago. 2.5 billion years is the age of the Aravallis in a later section.
o: 50 million years
5 million years
500 million years
2.5 billion years

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of the Himadri, the Greater Himalayas?
questions.a: The hill stations belong to the Himachal (Lower Himalayas). The Himadri is high, rugged, always snow-covered and thinly settled.
o: It has popular hill stations such as Shimla and Mussoorie
It is the highest and most rugged part of the range
It stays snow-covered throughout the whole year
It has very few settlements because life is tough

questions.q: The Fernandes family wants a holiday where the climate is moderate, there is rich biodiversity and people can live comfortably. They choose Darjeeling. Which Himalayan range is it in?
questions.a: Darjeeling is listed among the hill stations of the Himachal. Himadri is too cold and rugged; the Shivalik are lowest foothills; the Eastern Ghats are not Himalayan.
o: The Himachal, the Lower Himalayas
The Himadri, the Greater Himalayas
The Shivalik Hills, the Outer Himalayas
The Eastern Ghats, near the east coast

questions.q: In a classroom demonstration, Mr Pillai pushes one end of a carpet and it wrinkles upward in the middle. Which event in the chapter does this show?
questions.a: The chapter itself uses the carpet comparison for the Himalayas. The other options are formation of dunes, deltas and coral islands from later sections.
o: Land crumpling upward as India pushed against Eurasia
Wind shifting sand into hill-like dunes in a desert
A river dropping sediments at its mouth to build a triangular area
Coral skeletons piling up to form a ring of islands

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Himalayas and the source of the Ganga's stream.
1. India has always been joined to Eurasia, so the Himalayas formed along with the continent.
2. India is still pushing into Asia, very slowly, so the Himalayas are still growing taller.
3. The Bhagirathi, a tributary of the Ganga, originates from Gaumukh in Uttarakhand.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: India was part of Gondwana and broke away, moving north. 2 and 3 are as stated in the chapter.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Himalayas are sometimes called the 'Water Tower of Asia'.
Reason (R): In summer the snow on the mountains melts and feeds major rivers such as the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both true, and the snowmelt feeding the rivers is exactly why the Himalayas are called a water tower.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Where is the Great Himalayan National Park and what recognition has it received? (b) Who looks after its biodiversity?
questions.a: (a) In Himachal Pradesh; it is declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site. (b) The government as well as the village communities that live inside the park.
s: Part (a): Himachal Pradesh, UNESCO World Heritage Site
Part (b): government and village communities

questions.q: Where does the Bhagirathi originate? Give one reason why this place attracts visitors.
questions.a: At Gaumukh ('Cow's Mouth') in Uttarakhand, at the edge of the Gangotri Glacier. It is considered sacred and attracts pilgrims, and it is a popular trekking destination.
s: Names Gaumukh at the Gangotri Glacier in Uttarakhand
Gives one reason: sacred, pilgrims or trekking

questions.q: The chapter says the Himalayas rise about 5 mm each year. (a) By how many metres would they rise in 400 years at this rate? (b) Why do people not notice this rise in their lifetime?
questions.a: (a) 5 mm x 400 = 2000 mm = 2 metres. (b) The rise each year is tiny, only a few millimetres, so it is too small to see in one lifetime.
s: Part (a): 2 metres with the working shown
Part (b): yearly rise is a few millimetres, too slow to notice

questions.q: State two ways in which the snowmelt of the Himalayas helps the people who live along the rivers it feeds.
questions.a: The rivers and their tributaries provide water for drinking, farming and industrial use, supporting hundreds of millions of people.
s: First correct use of the river water
Second correct use of the river water

questions.q: Why is the kath-kuni style of house suited to the western Himalayas? Give two reasons.
questions.a: It uses locally available stone and wood, which keeps the house warm and resists damage in mild earthquakes.
s: Reason 1: made of local stone and wood, keeps warm
Reason 2: resists damage in mild earthquakes

questions.q: Sneha says, 'The Himalayas finished forming long ago, so they are no longer changing.' Do you agree? Support your answer with the figures in the chapter.
questions.a: No. India is still pushing into Asia at about 5 cm a year, and the Himalayas are still rising about 5 mm a year, which adds up to about 5 metres in a thousand years.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Evidence: India still pushes at about 5 cm a year
Evidence: Himalayas rise about 5 mm a year, about 5 m in a millennium

questions.q: A pamphlet says, 'The rocks of the Himalayas have stayed in the same place since India was joined to Africa, because land never moves.' Show using the chapter that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter says India was part of Gondwana, with Africa as its neighbour, then broke away and moved north. About 50 million years ago it collided with Eurasia and the land between crumpled and rose. India is still pushing into Asia today, so land does move.
s: Gondwana: India broke away from Africa's side and moved north
Collision about 50 million years ago made the land crumple and rise
India still pushes into Asia today, so the claim fails

questions.q: Few people live in the Himadri, but the Himachal has hill stations and human habitation. Give three reasons from the chapter that explain the difference.
questions.a: The Himadri is the highest and most rugged part, snow-covered throughout the year, so life is tough. The Himachal lies south of it, has a more moderate climate, and supports rich biodiversity and human habitation.
s: Himadri: highest and most rugged
Himadri: snow-covered all year, life is tough
Himachal: moderate climate allows biodiversity and habitation

questions.q: 'The Himalayas matter far beyond the mountains themselves.' Justify this statement with the water they supply, their meaning for people and their wildlife.
questions.a: Snowmelt feeds the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra, which give water for drinking, farming and industry to hundreds of millions, hence 'Water Tower of Asia'. The mountains are sacred, with temples and monasteries that draw monks and seekers. The Great Himalayan National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, protects diverse flora and fauna.
s: Water: snowmelt feeds the three major rivers
Culture and belief: sacred mountains, temples, monasteries
Biodiversity: Great Himalayan National Park, UNESCO site
Draws the conclusion that the range matters to millions beyond the mountains

questions.q: Compare the Himadri, the Himachal and the Shivalik Hills, and analyse how the Shivalik Hills link the high mountains to the plains.
questions.a: Himadri: highest and most rugged, home to Everest and Kanchenjunga, snow-covered all year. Himachal: south of it, more moderate climate, rich biodiversity, hill stations. Shivalik: outermost and lowest, rolling hills and dense forests rich in wildlife. Going south the height falls from the Himadri to the Shivalik, which are a transition zone between the Himalayas and the Gangetic Plains.
s: Himadri described with height and snow
Himachal described with climate and hill stations
Shivalik described as outermost, lowest, forested
Analysis: heights fall towards the south
Analysis: Shivalik as the transition zone to the Gangetic Plains

questions.q:
A museum in Dehradun has Rs 6 lakh for new Himalaya galleries. Options: 'Water Tower of Asia' Rs 4 lakh, 'How the mountains were formed' Rs 3 lakh, 'Life in the ranges' Rs 2 lakh. A survey of 200 visitors found that 90 want to know where the great rivers get their water, 70 want the story of how the mountains formed and 40 want to know how people and wildlife live in the mountains.
(a) Which three rivers, and the melting of what in which season, will the first gallery explain?
(b) What larger landmass was India once part of, and about how long ago did the collision shown in the second gallery happen?
(c) Give two exhibits the third gallery could carry, from the chapter.
(d) Which two galleries should the museum build, and why?
questions.a: (a) The Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra, fed by snow melting in summer. (b) Gondwana; about 50 million years ago. (c) Any two: kath-kuni houses, the Great Himalayan National Park, snow leopard, Himalayan monal, rhododendron sherbet. (d) Water Tower + Formation costs Rs 7 lakh, over budget. Water Tower + Life costs Rs 6 lakh and serves 90 + 40 = 130 visitors; Formation + Life costs Rs 5 lakh and serves 70 + 40 = 110. So build Water Tower and Life in the ranges.
s: Part (a): Ganga, Indus, Brahmaputra; summer snowmelt
Part (b): Gondwana, about 50 million years ago
Part (c): two exhibits such as kath-kuni houses, Great Himalayan National Park, monal, snow leopard, rhododendron sherbet
Part (d): Water Tower with Life in the ranges, backed by cost and visitors

questions.q:
The Rao family has two days in the Himalayas and a six-year-old child. Their list has three stops: a night in Shimla, a trek towards a snow-covered peak like Kanchenjunga, and a walk in the rolling, forested foothills just above the plains. Only two stops can be kept.
(a) Name the range in which each of the three stops lies.
(b) What climate does the Himachal have, and what does it allow?
(c) What does the chapter say about life in the range where the trek lies?
(d) Which stop should the family drop? Justify with chapter evidence.
questions.a: (a) Shimla - Himachal; Kanchenjunga trek - Himadri; forested foothills - Shivalik Hills. (b) A more moderate climate, allowing rich biodiversity and human habitation. (c) Life is tough, the region stays snow-covered all year and has few settlements. (d) Drop the Himadri trek: the family wants safe stays for a six-year-old, and the chapter says life there is tough, snow covers it all year and settlements are few, while Shimla (Himachal) is moderate and the Shivalik foothills are gentle forested hills.
s: Part (a): Himachal, Himadri, Shivalik matched to the stops
Part (b): moderate climate, rich biodiversity, human habitation
Part (c): Himadri life is tough, snow-covered all year, few settlements
Part (d): decision tied to the chapter

questions.q: Why does the chapter call Ladakh a 'cold desert'?
questions.a: Ladakh combines very little rain with winter temperatures below -30 degrees C. Dunes belong to the Thar; the rocks and the lake are real Ladakh facts but not what makes it a desert.
o: It has very little rainfall and winters below -30 degrees C
It has sand dunes up to 150 metres high and very hot days
Its folded rocks were once part of an ocean and are largely sand and clay
Its main lake, Pangong Tso, holds salty water carried from the mountains

questions.q: In the name Pangong Tso, what does 'tso' mean?
questions.a: The chapter explains that tso means lake.
o: Lake
Glacier
Valley
Monastery

questions.q: Which animal is reared in the Himalayas for milk, meat, wool and dung and is also used for transport?
questions.a: Yaks are the animal in the chapter. Ibex and Tibetan antelope are Ladakh's wildlife; the camel appears in the Thar section.
o: Yak
Ibex
Camel
Tibetan antelope

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a reason why the Gangetic Plains are fertile and densely populated?
questions.a: The ocean-origin folded rocks belong to Ladakh. The other three are reasons given for the plains.
o: Their folded rocks were once part of an ocean
Rivers from the Himalayas bring minerals that enrich the soil
The flat land allows roads and railways to link the region
Rivers supply water for drinking, farming and electricity

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with what the chapter says about it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Pangong Tso  2. Losar  3. Yak  4. Moonland
Column B: a. festival of the Ladakhi people  b. salty lake  c. animal used for transport  d. name for Ladakh's rocky terrain
questions.a: Pangong Tso is the salty lake, Losar a festival, the yak a transport animal and moonland the terrain. The distractors swap terrain with animal or lake with festival.

questions.q: A geologist at Leh sees rocky slopes made largely of sand and clay, carved into odd shapes. Which pair of facts from the chapter explains what he sees?
questions.a: The chapter says the folded portion was part of an ocean, so the rocks are mostly sand and clay, and wind and rain have eroded them. Lava, deltas and dunes belong to the islands, coasts and Thar.
o: The folded land was once part of an ocean, and wind and rain eroded it
The land is volcanic, and cooled lava has formed the odd shapes
Rivers deposit sediments at their mouths and pile them into pillars
Wind shifts loose sand into dunes that later harden into rock

questions.q: Two farmers compare notes. Gurpreet, in the Gangetic Plains, grows crops one after another on the same field in one year. Tsering, in Ladakh, cannot. Which feature of the plains best explains Gurpreet's advantage?
questions.a: The chapter says river minerals make the plains fertile and ideal for agriculture. Salty lakes, rocky valleys and yaks belong to the Himalayan and Ladakh sections.
o: Himalayan rivers bring minerals that enrich the soil
The salty water of a nearby lake feeds the fields
The deep valleys and rocky ground hold the water
The yaks of the plains supply dung to every field

questions.q:
Study the statements about the two regions.
1. Ladakh receives heavy rainfall and its winter temperatures stay above 0 degrees C.
2. The Gangetic Plains hold a small share of India's population because their flat land is hard to settle.
3. The flat land of the Northern Plains has helped build an elaborate network of roads and railways.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: Ladakh has very little rain and winters below -30 degrees C. 2 is false: a large proportion of India's population lives in the plains. 3 is stated in the chapter.
o: 3 only
1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Ladakh is a cold desert.
Reason (R): The rocks of Ladakh's folded mountains are made largely of sand and clay.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. The rocks are a fact about the terrain, but Ladakh is a desert because of very little rainfall, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Why is the terrain of Ladakh called 'moonland'? (b) What do geologists say caused this terrain?
questions.a: (a) It is rugged with rocky terrain and deep valleys and resembles the terrain of the moon. (b) The mountains were folded when the Indian landmass collided with Eurasia; the folded part had been under an ocean, so the rocks, largely sand and clay, were eroded by wind and rain.
s: Part (a): rocky, rugged, deep valleys, resembles the moon
Part (b): folding after the collision, ocean-origin rocks eroded by wind and rain

questions.q: (a) Name the lake in Ladakh whose water is salty. (b) Explain why its water is salty, unlike most other lakes.
questions.a: (a) Pangong Tso. (b) Minerals dissolve from the surrounding mountain areas into the water.
s: Part (a): Pangong Tso
Part (b): minerals dissolving from the surrounding mountains

questions.q: (a) Name two festivals of the Ladakhi people mentioned in the chapter. (b) What else is the region known for that makes it special for visitors?
questions.a: (a) Losar and the Hemis Festival. (b) Its ancient monasteries (and its unique wildlife).
s: Part (a): Losar and Hemis Festival
Part (b): ancient monasteries or unique wildlife

questions.q: State two reasons why the Gangetic Plains are ideal for agriculture.
questions.a: Rivers from the Himalayas provide water and bring minerals that enrich the soil, making it highly fertile.
s: Reason 1: water from the river systems
Reason 2: minerals brought by rivers enrich the soil

questions.q: (a) How has the flat land of the Northern Plains helped the movement of people and goods? (b) Besides water, name one thing the rivers of the plains bring or give.
questions.a: (a) The flat land allowed an elaborate transport network of roads and railways. (b) Minerals that enrich the soil, or electricity, or a route for travel and trade.
s: Part (a): flat land allowed road and rail networks
Part (b): minerals, electricity or a route for travel and trade

questions.q: Dev says, 'Ladakh is so cold that nothing can live there, so it is empty of people and animals.' Do you agree? Use the chapter to give reasons.
questions.a: No. The chapter names unique wildlife such as snow leopards, ibex and Tibetan antelopes, says the Ladakhi people lead a simple life with ancient monasteries and festivals such as Losar and Hemis, and describes yaks reared for milk, meat, wool and dung.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Names animals living there (snow leopard, ibex, Tibetan antelope)
Names people's life: yaks, monasteries or festivals

questions.q: Write a short three-line story about one day in a Ladakhi family's life in which the yak helps them in three different ways. Name the use in each line.
questions.a: Any story that shows three of: milk or meat for food, wool for clothing, dung (as fuel/manure), carrying loads for transport.
s: First use of the yak shown correctly
Second use, different from the first
Third use, different from the first two

questions.q: A railway planner is asked why new lines should be laid across the Gangetic Plains rather than the rocky land of Ladakh. Give three reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: The plains are flat, which has already allowed an elaborate road and rail network; a large proportion of India's population lives there; the fertile, river-fed land produces abundant farm goods to carry. Ladakh has rocky terrain and deep valleys.
s: Flat land suits roads and railways
Large population lives in the plains
Fertile land and rivers support farming and trade

questions.q: Compare the cold desert of Ladakh and the Gangetic Plains under rainfall or water, terrain, farming and life of the people, and analyse why one supports far more people.
questions.a: Ladakh: very little rainfall, winter below -30 degrees C, rocky terrain and deep valleys, yaks for livelihood; few people. Plains: Himalayan rivers bring water and minerals, flat land, fertile soil, abundant farming, transport; a large share of India's population. A large share of India's population lives in the plains because of the fertile land and water, while Ladakh's cold, little rain and rocky terrain make life depend on animals like the yak.
s: Ladakh's climate and terrain described
Plains' water, soil and flat land described
Contrast in farming or livelihood (yaks vs agriculture)
Analysis: links resources to population

questions.q: Suppose the Himalayas did not exist. Using the chapter, discuss what would happen to the rivers, farming and population of the Gangetic Plains.
questions.a: The Himalayas feed the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra with snowmelt, which is why they are the 'Water Tower of Asia'. Without them the rivers would lose their source and the minerals they bring would no longer enrich the soil, so the plains would not stay highly fertile. Farming and electricity from the rivers would suffer, and the large share of India's population that depends on the plains would lose water and food.
s: Himalayan snowmelt feeds the three river systems
Minerals carried by rivers enrich the soil, which would be lost
Farming and electricity would suffer
Large population depends on the plains
Reaches a clear conclusion

questions.q:
Students of a Chennai school plan a stall called 'Ladakh Day' to show how a cold desert differs from a hot one. Their notes: winters fall to about -32 degrees C; the land is rocky with deep valleys; one lake has salty water; families keep yaks. The stall has room for only one main display: the winter cold, the salty lake or the yaks.
(a) Why is Ladakh called a desert although it is so cold?
(b) What explains the salty water of Pangong Tso?
(c) Give two ways in which yaks support Ladakhi families.
(d) Which display best meets the stall's aim, and why?
questions.a: (a) Because it receives very little rainfall. (b) Minerals dissolve from the surrounding mountain areas into the lake. (c) Any two of milk, meat, wool, dung and transport. (d) The winter cold: the stall's aim is the difference from a hot desert, and winters below -30 degrees C against the Thar's very hot days show that contrast best; the lake and the yaks show features of Ladakh but not the contrast.
s: Part (a): very little rainfall
Part (b): minerals dissolving from surrounding mountains
Part (c): two uses of the yak
Part (d): winter cold display, justified by contrast with hot desert

questions.q:
The Mehta family farms near the Ganga in Uttar Pradesh. Their field grows paddy in the monsoon and another crop afterwards. Their village has good connections to the district town and steady electricity. The panchayat has one piece of land near the river and must choose between a new farm plot and a warehouse close to the main railway line. The gram sabha has said its first aim is to raise food output for the village's large population.
(a) Which feature of the river water helps the Mehtas' soil stay fertile?
(b) Explain how the flat land and the rivers of the plains help with transport and with power.
(c) Give one argument from the chapter for the farm plot and one for the warehouse.
(d) Which should the panchayat choose, given the gram sabha's aim?
questions.a: (a) The rivers bring minerals that enrich the soil. (b) Flat land allowed road and rail networks; rivers have long carried travel and trade and are a source of electricity. (c) Farm plot: fertile, mineral-rich soil, ideal for agriculture. Warehouse: flat land has produced an elaborate road and rail network. (d) The farm plot: the first aim is food output, and the chapter says the river-fed soil is highly fertile and ideal for agriculture; the warehouse can follow later because the rail network already exists.
s: Part (a): minerals brought from the Himalayas
Part (b): road and rail on flat land, rivers for travel, trade and electricity
Part (c): one argument for each option
Part (d): farm plot, tied to the stated aim

questions.q: The Pushkar Mela, where camel vendors gather, is held
questions.a: The chapter places the Pushkar Mela at the edge of the Thar. Jaisalmer is the fort-city in the middle of the desert; Mount Abu is the Aravallis' highest peak.
o: at the edge of the Thar Desert
in the middle of the Thar Desert
on the highest peak of the Aravallis
beside the zinc mines at Zawar

questions.q: What are taanka or kunds, which Rajasthan is famous for?
questions.a: Taanka or kunds store rainwater, often for drinking. The other options are the sand-cleaning habit, the forts and the Zawar mines from the same section.
o: Special rainwater collection systems
Pits where utensils are scoured with sand
Forts in the hills built to stop enemies
Mines where zinc was first extracted

questions.q: Which important role do the Aravallis play for northwestern India?
questions.a: The Aravallis act as a natural barrier against the desert's eastward spread. The Himalayas separate India from the continent and give snowmelt; the Deccan lies between the Ghats.
o: They stop the Thar Desert from spreading further east
They separate India from the rest of the continent
They feed the Indus and Brahmaputra with snowmelt
They lie between the two Ghats and form the Deccan

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT named in the chapter among the minerals of the Aravallis?
questions.a: The Aravallis are rich in marble, granite, zinc and copper. Coal is a plateau resource shown with the coal mines of the Peninsular Plateau.
o: Coal
Marble
Zinc
Copper

questions.q: Meera travels from Kumbhalgarh Fort to the 'Golden City' of Jaisalmer in a day. Which change in landscape does she go through?
questions.a: Kumbhalgarh stands in the Aravallis, and Jaisalmer lies in the middle of the Thar. The other pairs are real chapter landforms from other regions.
o: From the Aravalli Hills into the Thar Desert
From the Western Ghats into the Deccan Plateau
From the Shivalik Hills into the Gangetic Plains
From the Eastern Ghats onto the east coast plain

questions.q: A building firm in Jaipur wants marble and granite, and a metals firm wants zinc and copper, both from one old hill range in the northwest. Which range does the chapter point to?
questions.a: The chapter says the Aravallis are rich in marble, granite, zinc and copper. The other ranges are described for forests, biodiversity or low broken hills.
o: The Aravallis, which have supported mining for centuries
The Shivalik Hills, rich in forests and wildlife
The Western Ghats, home to rivers and biodiversity
The Eastern Ghats, lower hills along the east coast

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Thar and the Aravallis.
1. Most of the Thar lies within India, spanning Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab and Haryana.
2. The Aravallis are among the oldest mountains in the world, about 2.5 billion years old.
3. The Aravallis are young fold mountains that are still rising by about 5 mm every year.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 is false: the 5 mm yearly rise belongs to the Himalayas; the Aravallis are about 2.5 billion years old.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the Thar Desert, utensils are traditionally cleaned by scouring them with sand.
Reason (R): Water is scarce in the desert and women often travel long distances to fetch it.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, and scarcity of water is the reason sand is used and only a little water kept for rinsing.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) How are sand dunes formed? (b) A mountain keeps its shape for millions of years, yet a dune keeps changing. Why?
questions.a: (a) The wind shifts and shapes sand into hill-like formations. (b) Mountains are made of rock so their shape is fixed, but dunes are loose sand that the wind keeps moving.
s: Part (a): the wind shifts and shapes the sand
Part (b): rock mountains have a fixed shape, loose sand is moved by wind

questions.q: Which fort-city is called the 'Golden City', where is it located and why is it recognised worldwide?
questions.a: Jaisalmer, in the middle of the Thar Desert; its fort is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
s: Names Jaisalmer in the middle of the Thar
Its fort is a UNESCO World Heritage site

questions.q: State two features of the Thar that make it a natural barrier to the movement of people and animals.
questions.a: Very high daytime temperatures with cold nights, and a lack of access to water.
s: Names any one condition: high daytime heat, cold nights or lack of water
Names a second, different condition from the same list

questions.q: (a) What are taanka or kunds? (b) Why are they especially valuable in a place where women walk long distances to fetch water?
questions.a: (a) Special water collection systems that store rainwater, often for drinking. (b) They keep water close to home, reducing the long daily trips to fetch water.
s: Part (a): rainwater collection and storage systems, often for drinking
Part (b): saves the long daily journey for water

questions.q: (a) Name two minerals found in the Aravallis. (b) What does the evidence from the Zawar mines show about Indians of the past?
questions.a: (a) Any two of marble, granite, zinc, copper. (b) Over eight centuries ago Indians were the first in the world to master the delicate process of extracting zinc.
s: Part (a): two correct minerals
Part (b): early mastery of zinc extraction at Zawar

questions.q: Isha says, 'The Aravallis stop the Thar from spreading east, so no part of Haryana can belong to the desert.' Is she right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The Aravallis prevent the desert from expanding further eastward, but the Thar already spans Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab and Haryana. Stopping further spread is not the same as removing the desert from a state.
s: Verdict: not right
Aravallis prevent further eastward spread of the Thar
The Thar spans Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab and Haryana, so Haryana has desert

questions.q: A tourism brochure says, 'In the Thar, water is plentiful, so people have no need to save it.' Show with two facts from the chapter that this cannot be right.
questions.a: Water is scarce in the desert: women often travel long distances every day to fetch it. People clean utensils with sand, use a little water for a light rinse and reuse that water for plants, and store rainwater in taanka or kunds. None of this would be needed if water were plentiful.
s: Water is scarce, with long trips to fetch it
Gives a saving habit such as the sand cleaning and rinse reuse
Gives taanka or kunds storing rainwater and concludes the claim fails

questions.q: What does the chapter say about the location of Kumbhalgarh Fort, and which two other forts does it name in the same hills?
questions.a: Its location in the hills proved to be an excellent deterrent to the enemy, as it is surrounded by the Aravallis. Chittorgarh and Ranthambore are the other forts.
s: Fort is surrounded by the Aravalli Hills
Location in the hills proved an excellent deterrent to the enemy
Names Chittorgarh and Ranthambore

questions.q: 'The Aravallis shape the geography and the human history of northwestern India.' Justify this statement with at least four points from the chapter.
questions.a: They are among the world's oldest mountains; they act as a barrier stopping the Thar from spreading east; they are rich in marble, granite, zinc and copper, supporting mining and construction for centuries; Zawar shows early zinc extraction; forts like Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh and Ranthambore stand here.
s: Age and range of the Aravallis
Barrier against the eastward spread of the Thar
Mineral wealth and mining for centuries
Zawar zinc extraction
Forts built in the hills

questions.q: Suppose the monsoon fails for a whole year in a Thar village. Which of the water practices in the chapter would still work, which would not, and what does this show about the way people have adapted to the desert?
questions.a: Scouring utensils with sand, using only a little water for a light rinse and reusing it for plants would still work, since they save water that is available. Taanka or kunds store rainwater, so they would stay empty if no rain fell. People adapt by combining saving habits with storage; the saving habits matter most when the rain fails.
s: Sand cleaning and light rinse still work
Rinse reuse for plants still works
Taanka or kunds depend on rain so would stay empty
Explains that habits save available water while storage needs rain
Concludes on how people adapt, linking to water scarcity

questions.q:
In a Thar village the Bhati family of 5 depends on a covered tank dug into the ground, which fills during the monsoon and is meant mostly for drinking. The tank holds 9,000 litres and the family uses 6 litres per person per day. The next monsoon arrives after 365 days. A second tank of 2,000 litres would cost Rs 15,000. The other choice is to adopt desert water habits that would cut use by 2 litres per person per day at no cost.
(a) What is this kind of rainwater collection system called in Rajasthan?
(b) For how many days will the full tank last at present?
(c) By how many days or litres does the present supply fall short of the 365 days?
(d) Compare the two choices with numbers and decide which the elder should recommend.
questions.a: (a) A taanka or kund. (b) Daily use is 5 x 6 = 30 litres, so 9000 / 30 = 300 days. (c) 365 - 300 = 65 days; 65 x 30 = 1950 litres. (d) Habits: use falls to 5 x 4 = 20 litres a day, so 9000 / 20 = 450 days, enough for 365 with 85 days spare, at no cost. Second tank: 11000 / 30 = about 366.7 days, barely enough, and costs Rs 15,000. Recommend the habits.
s: Part (a): taanka or kund
Part (b): 9000 divided by 30 gives 300 days
Part (c): 65 days short, 1950 litres
Part (d): habits last 450 days, second tank 366.7 days, so habits recommended

questions.q:
A Delhi school plans a one-day visit for 40 students to study 'How people used the Aravalli Hills'. The grant is Rs 25,000, and the principal's rule is that all 40 students must go. Site A is the Zawar mines at Rs 700 per student. Site B is the Chittorgarh fort at Rs 500 per student.
(a) Name two minerals of the Aravallis and say what they have supported for centuries.
(b) What does the evidence from Zawar show?
(c) Which sites fit the grant when all 40 go?
(d) Which site should the school choose, and what does the chapter say about hill forts like it?
questions.a: (a) Any two of marble, granite, zinc, copper; they have supported mining and construction activities for centuries. (b) Over eight centuries ago Indians were the first in the world to master the extraction of zinc. (c) Zawar: 40 x 700 = Rs 28,000, over the grant. Chittorgarh: 40 x 500 = Rs 20,000, within it. (d) Chittorgarh: it is the only site that fits the grant with all 40 students, and the chapter lists it among the hill forts of the Aravallis, whose hill locations served as a deterrent to the enemy.
s: Part (a): two minerals; mining and construction
Part (b): early zinc extraction
Part (c): Zawar Rs 28,000 is over; Chittorgarh Rs 20,000 fits
Part (d): Chittorgarh, with the chapter's point about hill forts

questions.q: Why is the triangular plateau of southern India called a 'peninsular' plateau?
questions.a: A peninsula is land surrounded by water on three sides: the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal and the Indian Ocean. The two Ghats border the plateau but do not define a peninsula.
o: It is surrounded by water on three sides
It lies between the Western and Eastern Ghats
It is surrounded by water on all four sides
It rises between two seas and the Himalayas

questions.q: Which statement about the two mountain ranges bordering the Peninsular Plateau is correct?
questions.a: The Western Ghats run like a wall along the west coast and are taller; the Eastern Ghats are lower and broken. Other options reverse the heights or the sides.
o: The Western Ghats are taller, while the Eastern Ghats are lower and broken into smaller hills
The Eastern Ghats are taller, while the Western Ghats are lower and broken into smaller hills
Both ranges are of equal height and run unbroken along the two coasts
The Western Ghats are lower and run along the east, the Eastern Ghats along the west

questions.q: Which of the following rivers does NOT flow into the Bay of Bengal?
questions.a: The Tapti, like the Narmada, is a west-flowing river that drains into the Arabian Sea. The Godavari, Krishna and Mahanadi are east-flowing.
o: Tapti
Godavari
Krishna
Mahanadi

questions.q: Which of the following is a tribal community of the dense forests of the Peninsular Plateau?
questions.a: The chapter names the Santhal, Gond, Baiga, Bhil and Korku. Khasi and Garo belong to the hills of the Northeast, and Ladakhi to Ladakh.
o: Baiga
Khasi
Ladakhi
Garo

questions.q:
Match each feature in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Western Ghats  2. Eastern Ghats  3. Deccan Plateau  4. Narmada and Tapti
Column B: a. lower hills broken along the eastern coast  b. vast area of flat highlands between the ranges  c. taller range running like a wall along the west  d. rivers draining into the Arabian Sea
questions.a: Western Ghats - taller range along the west; Eastern Ghats - lower and broken; Deccan - flat highlands; Narmada and Tapti - west-flowing. Distractors swap the two Ghats or the Deccan with the rivers.

questions.q: Ishaan studies the physical map and sees that the Godavari, Krishna and Mahanadi flow across the plateau towards the Bay of Bengal. Which feature does the chapter give to explain this?
questions.a: The chapter says the plateau tilts a little to the east. The Eastern Ghats are the lower range, and the plateau is surrounded by water on three sides, not one.
o: The plateau tilts a little to the east
The Eastern Ghats are the taller range
The triangular plateau narrows towards the Bay of Bengal
The plateau is surrounded by water only on the east

questions.q: At Periyakanal near Munnar in Kerala, a powerhouse runs on a waterfall. Why do plateaus have waterfalls like this?
questions.a: The chapter says waterfalls form as rivers flow over uneven, rocky plateau surfaces, and they help in hydroelectric power. Snowmelt belongs to the Himalayas; tides and coral reefs belong to the coasts and islands.
o: Rivers flow over uneven and rocky plateau surfaces
Snowmelt drops from glacier edges onto the plateau
Tides from the Arabian Sea push water up the valleys
Waves break on coral reefs lying off the plateau

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Peninsular Plateau.
1. The Peninsular Plateau is a recent land formation, younger than the Himalayas.
2. East-flowing rivers such as the Godavari, Krishna and Mahanadi originate on the plateau.
3. The Deccan Plateau lies outside the Ghats, on the side facing the sea.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: the plateau is described as a very old land formation. 3 is false: the Deccan Plateau lies between the two ranges. 2 is stated in the chapter.
o: 2 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The dense forests of the plateau are home to tribal communities such as the Gond and the Bhil.
Reason (R): All the tribal communities of India live on the Peninsular Plateau.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true. R is false: the chapter shows tribal communities are spread over many states, and the Khasi of the Northeast hills are another example.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What is a plateau? (b) Why is the large plateau of southern India described as 'peninsular'?
questions.a: (a) A landform that rises above the surrounding land with a more or less flat surface, some of its sides often steep slopes. (b) It is surrounded by water on three sides - the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal and the Indian Ocean.
s: Part (a): raised, more or less flat surface with steep sides
Part (b): surrounded by water on three sides, naming the water bodies

questions.q: Name three tribal communities that live in the dense forests of the plateau and state what the chapter says about their way of life.
questions.a: Any three of Santhal, Gond, Baiga, Bhil, Korku. They have distinct languages, traditions and ways of life closely connected to Nature.
s: Names three correct communities
Distinct languages and traditions closely connected to Nature

questions.q: (a) Name the two west-flowing rivers the chapter mentions. (b) Into which water body do they drain, and how does this differ from the Godavari?
questions.a: (a) Narmada and Tapti. (b) They drain into the Arabian Sea, while the east-flowing Godavari drains into the Bay of Bengal.
s: Part (a): Narmada and Tapti
Part (b): Arabian Sea versus the Bay of Bengal for the Godavari

questions.q: State two ways in which the waterfalls of the plateau are useful to people.
questions.a: They attract tourists, help generate hydroelectric power and provide water for irrigation.
s: First use of waterfalls
Second use of waterfalls

questions.q: (a) Why is coal an important resource of the plateau? (b) What caution does the chapter attach to its use?
questions.a: (a) It is an important resource, especially in the production of electricity. (b) Coal is a fossil fuel, the use of which contributes to global warming.
s: Part (a): coal produces electricity
Part (b): fossil fuel use contributes to global warming

questions.q: Tanvi lists five rivers from the chapter - Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi, Narmada and Tapti - and says, 'Three of these five flow west.' Check her count and say what the chapter tells us about the direction of each.
questions.a: She is wrong. Godavari, Krishna and Mahanadi are east-flowing, draining towards the Bay of Bengal, because the plateau tilts a little to the east. Only the Narmada and Tapti flow west into the Arabian Sea, so two flow west and three east.
s: Verdict: the count is wrong
Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi flow east to the Bay of Bengal
Narmada and Tapti flow west to the Arabian Sea, so two not three

questions.q: Frame three short questions whose answers are (i) the Western Ghats, (ii) the Eastern Ghats and (iii) the Deccan Plateau. Each question must give one clue from the chapter.
questions.a: E.g. (i) Which taller range runs like a wall along the west coast? (ii) Which lower, broken range lies along the eastern coast? (iii) Which vast area of flat highlands lies between the two ranges?
s: Question (i) has a correct clue for the Western Ghats
Question (ii) has a correct clue for the Eastern Ghats
Question (iii) has a correct clue for the Deccan Plateau

questions.q: Give three reasons why the Western Ghats are special, according to the chapter.
questions.a: They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site; they are home to many rivers; they have rich biodiversity, such as the lion-tailed macaque, the king cobra and an insect-eating plant.
s: UNESCO World Heritage Site
Home to many rivers
Rich biodiversity with an example

questions.q: 'The Peninsular Plateau has helped India's economy and its people in many ways.' Justify the statement with minerals, rivers, forests, waterfalls and tribal communities.
questions.a: Minerals such as coal supply electricity; rivers give water to millions and power; forests are home to tribal communities such as the Santhal and Gond with distinct traditions; waterfalls give tourists, hydroelectric power and irrigation; fertile land supports farming.
s: Minerals (coal) and electricity
Rivers for farming, industry and hydroelectric power
Forests and tribal communities
Waterfalls: tourism, power, irrigation
Draws a justified conclusion

questions.q: Anika travels from the Arabian Sea coast to the Bay of Bengal across the Peninsular Plateau. List in order the features she crosses and describe each in one line using the chapter.
questions.a: Arabian Sea coast, then the Western Ghats (taller, like a wall along the west coast, waterfalls in the monsoon), then the Deccan Plateau (a vast area of flat highlands), then the Eastern Ghats (lower and broken into smaller hills along the east coast), then the Bay of Bengal.
s: Gives the order: Western Ghats, Deccan Plateau, Eastern Ghats
Western Ghats described: taller, wall-like, along the west coast
Deccan Plateau described: vast flat highlands between the ranges
Eastern Ghats described: lower and broken, along the east coast

questions.q:
A state power board must choose one new plant: a hydroelectric plant on a plateau waterfall river in the Western Ghats region, costing Rs 400 crore, or a coal-fired plant near a plateau coal mine, costing Rs 300 crore. The board has publicly pledged to cut its contribution to global warming.
(a) Why does the Peninsular Plateau have so many waterfalls?
(b) Besides electricity, what two other benefits do the waterfalls give?
(c) What harm does the chapter link with coal?
(d) Which plant should the board build, and why, in spite of the cost difference?
questions.a: (a) Rivers flow over the uneven and rocky surfaces of the plateau. (b) They attract tourists and provide water for irrigation. (c) Coal is a fossil fuel and its use contributes to global warming. (d) The hydroelectric plant: the board's pledge is about global warming, which coal worsens, and the waterfall also brings tourism and irrigation; the Rs 100 crore saving on coal does not meet the pledge.
s: Part (a): rivers over uneven rocky surfaces
Part (b): tourists and irrigation water
Part (c): fossil fuel contributes to global warming
Part (d): hydroelectric plant, tied to the pledge

questions.q:
A Santhal village in Jharkhand lives beside a dense forest of 500 hectares on the plateau. A company proposes a coal mine that would clear 40 per cent of the forest and promises jobs for ten years. The gram sabha's rule is that it will accept only a project that does not threaten the forest on which its languages and traditions depend.
(a) Name two other tribal communities of the plateau's forests.
(b) Why is the plateau a likely place for mining?
(c) What harm does the chapter link with coal?
(d) How many hectares would the mine clear, and what should the gram sabha decide under its rule?
questions.a: (a) Any two of Gond, Baiga, Bhil, Korku. (b) The plateau is rich in minerals, including coal. (c) Coal is a fossil fuel and its use contributes to global warming. (d) 40 per cent of 500 = 200 hectares cleared, leaving 300. The mine threatens the forest tied to the community's traditions, and coal adds to global warming, so under the rule the gram sabha should refuse.
s: Part (a): two of Gond, Baiga, Bhil, Korku
Part (b): rich in minerals
Part (c): fossil fuel contributes to global warming
Part (d): 200 hectares cleared; reject under the rule

questions.q: Which of the following describes a delta, as the chapter explains it?
questions.a: A delta forms from river sediments at the mouth. The other options are the chapter's lagoon, archipelago and peninsula, which students often confuse with a delta.
o: A fan-shaped area built by a river's sediments at its mouth
A body of water separated from larger waters by a natural barrier
A group of islands scattered across a sea, such as Lakshadweep
A piece of land surrounded by water on three of its sides

questions.q: The east coast of India lies between the Eastern Ghats and
questions.a: The east coast lies between the Eastern Ghats and the Bay of Bengal. The Arabian Sea lies on the west and the Western Ghats run along the west coast.
o: the Bay of Bengal
the Arabian Sea
the Indian Ocean
the Western Ghats

questions.q: Which statement about the Andaman and Nicobar Islands is NOT correct?
questions.a: The 36 coral islands near Kerala are Lakshadweep. The other statements are in the chapter.
o: They are made up of 36 coral islands near the coast of Kerala
They are more than 500 large and small volcanic islands
Barren Island among them is the only active volcano in India
They hold Cellular Jail, where freedom fighters were imprisoned

questions.q: Which part of India does the chapter say receives one of the highest rainfalls in the world?
questions.a: The hills of the Northeast, on the Meghalaya Plateau, are known for heavy rainfall. The Thar is the arid region of the chapter.
o: The Meghalaya Plateau hills of the Northeast
The Sundarbans in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta region
The east coast plains around the Mahanadi delta
The Thar Desert and Aravalli Hills region

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with the correct description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Chilika and Pulicat  2. Barren Island  3. Mawlynnong  4. Sundarbans
Column B: a. village called the cleanest in Asia  b. lakes of the east coast  c. India's only active volcano  d. delta shared with another country, home of the Royal Bengal Tiger
questions.a: Chilika and Pulicat - east-coast lakes; Barren Island - the active volcano; Mawlynnong - cleanest village; Sundarbans - shared delta with the tiger.

questions.q: Rekha's family grows paddy on flat, fertile land near the point where the Krishna meets the Bay of Bengal. Her teacher says the land itself is the work of the river. Which process does the chapter give for such land?
questions.a: The chapter explains deltas as sediments deposited by a river at its mouth, building up triangular or fan-shaped land that is fertile. Coral, dunes and folding are the processes of islands, the Thar and the Himalayas.
o: The river deposits sediments at its mouth, building up land
Waves and tides heap up coral skeletons into new land
Wind keeps shifting loose sand into hill-like formations
Rock layers crumple upward when two landmasses collide

questions.q: An officer is asked why tiny Lakshadweep islands, many of them uninhabited, matter to India. Which reason from the chapter is correct?
questions.a: The chapter says that India controls a vast marine area through them, allowing fishing, resource exploration and environmental protection. The volcano is on Barren Island and the shared delta is the Sundarbans.
o: India controls a vast sea area through them, useful for fishing
They are densely populated, with India's biggest island cities
They hold the only active volcano found in India's territory
They lie in the Ganga delta, shared with Bangladesh as a border

questions.q:
Study the statements about India's coasts and islands.

questions.a: All three are stated in the chapter.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Sundarbans lie entirely within India.
Reason (R): The Sundarbans are located in the delta of the Ganga, the Brahmaputra and their tributaries.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: about half is in India and the rest in Bangladesh. R is true.

questions.q: (a) How is a delta formed? (b) Why are the deltas of the Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri and Mahanadi useful for farming?
questions.a: (a) When a river deposits sediments into a larger water body at its mouth, they build up into a triangular or fan-shaped area. (b) The land is fertile, making it ideal for farming.
s: Part (a): river deposits sediments at its mouth, building a triangular or fan-shaped area
Part (b): fertile land ideal for farming

questions.q: Differentiate between Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in terms of the sea they lie in and the way they are made.
questions.a: Lakshadweep lies in the Arabian Sea and is made of 36 coral islands. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie in the Bay of Bengal and are more than 500 volcanic islands.
s: Lakshadweep: Arabian Sea, coral
Andaman and Nicobar: Bay of Bengal, volcanic

questions.q: (a) In which river delta do the Sundarbans lie? (b) Why does the protection of this delta involve two countries?
questions.a: (a) The delta of the Ganga, Brahmaputra and their tributaries. (b) About half of it lies in India and the rest is in Bangladesh.
s: Part (a): Ganga-Brahmaputra delta
Part (b): shared, half in India and the rest in Bangladesh

questions.q: State two features of the hills of the Northeast on the Meghalaya Plateau.
questions.a: Lush greenery, heavy rainfall (one of the highest in the world), breathtaking waterfalls, rich forests, unique wildlife and fertile land.
s: First correct feature
Second correct feature

questions.q: State two features of the rivers and the coastline of the west coast of India.
questions.a: Most rivers originate in the Western Ghats and flow swiftly to form estuaries; the coast has coves, creeks and estuaries, with the Narmada and Tapti estuaries being the largest.
s: Rivers: from the Western Ghats, swift, forming estuaries
Coast: coves, creeks, estuaries, largest Narmada and Tapti

questions.q: Arjun says, 'The west coast and the east coast of India are alike, with wide plains and big deltas on both.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. The west coast, from Gujarat to Kerala, has short, swift rivers from the Western Ghats forming estuaries, with the Western Ghats close to the sea. The east coast, between the Eastern Ghats and the Bay of Bengal, has wide plains and deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri.
s: Verdict: disagrees
West coast: swift short rivers forming estuaries
East coast: wide plains and major deltas

questions.q: A student claims that Lakshadweep has more islands than the Andaman and Nicobar group. Show, using the chapter's numbers, that this cannot be right.
questions.a: Lakshadweep has 36 islands; the Andaman and Nicobar group has more than 500. Even taking exactly 500, 500 - 36 = 464 more, so the claim is impossible.
s: Gives 36 for Lakshadweep and more than 500 for the Andaman and Nicobar
Calculates the difference as at least 464
Concludes that the claim is impossible

questions.q: Describe three ways in which the people of the Northeast hills show a close bond with Nature, using examples from the chapter.
questions.a: The Khasi people celebrate the Shad Suk Mynsiem festival to show gratitude towards nature; living root bridges are made by weaving tree roots over many years; Mawlynnong has bamboo dustbins and eco-friendly living.
s: Example 1: Shad Suk Mynsiem festival of gratitude to nature
Example 2: living root bridges made of woven roots
Example 3: eco-friendly living, bamboo dustbins in Mawlynnong

questions.q: Compare the west coast and the east coast of India, and analyse why the deltas of the east coast matter for farming.
questions.a: West: from Gujarat to Kerala, rivers from the Western Ghats flow swiftly, forming estuaries, coves and creeks, Narmada and Tapti estuaries the largest, important ports. East: between the Eastern Ghats and the Bay of Bengal, wide plains and deltas of Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, lakes Chilika and Pulicat. Deltas are built of river sediments, making land fertile and ideal for farming.
s: West coast: extent and rivers forming estuaries
East coast: wide plains and deltas, lakes
Delta formation by river sediments
Analysis: fertile land makes deltas ideal for farming

questions.q: The Sundarbans are described as a delta with 'a unique combination of the river, sea and land'. Justify this description with four points from the chapter.
questions.a: The Sundarbans lie in the delta of the Ganga, Brahmaputra and their tributaries, where river, sea and land meet. About half is in India and the rest in Bangladesh. Mangroves grow in the delta. It is home to many species, including the Royal Bengal Tiger. It is a UNESCO Heritage site.
s: Location in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta where river, sea and land meet
Shared between India and Bangladesh
Mangroves of the delta
Wildlife such as the Royal Bengal Tiger
UNESCO Heritage site, concluding the description is justified

questions.q:
A school in Visakhapatnam plans a two-day field trip for a project called 'How rivers create farmland near the sea'. It can visit only one coast. The west-coast plan covers the estuaries of the Narmada and Tapti and the port city of Mumbai. The east-coast plan covers the delta region of the Godavari and the area around Chilika Lake.
(a) How is a delta formed, and what is a lagoon, according to the chapter?
(b) What kind of coastline do the short, swift rivers of the west coast create?
(c) Why are the deltas of the Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri and Mahanadi valuable for people?
(d) Which plan should the school choose for this project, and why?
questions.a: (a) A delta forms where a river deposits sediments at its mouth, building a triangular or fan-shaped area. A lagoon is a body of water separated from larger bodies of water by a natural barrier. (b) Coves, creeks and estuaries, the Narmada and Tapti estuaries being the largest. (c) Their fertile land makes them ideal for farming. (d) The east-coast plan: the project is about farmland, and the chapter says the deltas of the east coast are fertile and ideal for farming, while the west-coast features are estuaries and ports.
s: Part (a): delta from river sediments; lagoon separated by a natural barrier
Part (b): estuaries, coves and creeks
Part (c): fertile land ideal for farming
Part (d): east-coast plan, tied to farmland

questions.q:
A village council in the East Khasi Hills must provide a safe crossing over a stream in a region of very heavy rainfall before the next monsoon, six months away. Option A is a concrete bridge. Option B is a bridge of living tree roots, like those in neighbouring villages. The council also has a small heritage fund.
(a) Which plateau do the Khasi hills belong to?
(b) What does the chapter say living root bridges show about the tribes of the Northeast?
(c) How are such bridges made, and how long does it take?
(d) With a six-month deadline, which option should the council use for the crossing, and what could it do with the heritage fund?
questions.a: (a) The Meghalaya Plateau. (b) They show the craftsmanship of the tribes of the Northeast. (c) Tree roots are woven together over the course of many years. (d) Build the concrete bridge for the monsoon, since a root bridge takes many years; use the heritage fund to start growing a root bridge nearby, keeping the tribal craft and attracting visitors.
s: Part (a): Meghalaya Plateau
Part (b): craftsmanship of the tribes
Part (c): weaving tree roots over many years
Part (d): concrete bridge now, root bridge started as heritage
